What we do not yet know: how many people have been removed without final orders since January 2025, whether the pattern concentrates in specific detention circuits, and whether habeas remedies are functioning at scale or only for the rare cases that reach federal court.

Credit where due: the Deportation Data Project, led by David Hausman and collaborators, is doing some of the most important independent data work on removals. Their FOIA spreadsheets are the reason these cases are visible at all.

NY1 sent the data to EOIR before publishing. A spokesperson declined to comment on third-party analysis of EOIR data. DOJ did not respond to questions about the Salvadoran man's case. Outside reporting and FOIA work is effectively the only audit available right now.

The deportations are happening faster than the legal architecture was built to process. ICE's stated removal target is 3,000 per day. Roughly 60,000 people are currently detained. The administrative mechanisms designed to secure due process are being bypassed or outrun.

Sheila McNulty served 16 years at DOJ and was Chief Immigration Judge when she was dismissed on the first day of Trump's second term. She told NY1 she does not know the legal basis for deporting people without final orders: "I'm not sure where the authority is."

One case: a Salvadoran man with Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and a pending green card was arrested in New York, flown to Texas, and deported to El Salvador with no final removal order on record. His attorney, Ed Cuccia, described the removal as unlawful.

Noncitizens are being deported without final removal orders, which immigration attorneys say is flatly illegal. Lawyers in New York, Louisiana, Texas, and Illinois have reported such cases to NY1. At least two of the documented deportations occurred in New York City.

What we do not yet know: how many of the ten Ohio departments are operating outside their jurisdictions, whether federal funding supports their operations, and how ambient enforcement behavior is reshaping public life in counties with no formal agreement.

The chilling effect does not stop at the jurisdictional line. When a 287(g) officer from a town of 850 can appear at a Cincinnati school and invoke ICE, the functional reach of the program exceeds its formal map. That geography is not captured in the ICE registry.

For scale: ICE reports 1,697 active 287(g) agreements as of April 17, 2026, across 39 states, up from roughly 135 before January 2025. Oversight and training capacity has not scaled with the program. The Gratis case is what that gap looks like on the ground.

The story is being read as a rogue-officer problem. The Enquirer's reporting suggests something broader: a pattern of very small departments signing federal enforcement agreements in the last six months, with unclear geographic scope and unclear federal funding.

Gratis is a village of roughly 850 residents in Preble County. Its police department signed a 287(g) Task Force Model agreement in November 2025. Its jurisdiction does not extend to Hamilton County. The chief and one other officer are now on administrative leave.

Ten Ohio police departments serving towns of fewer than 2,500 people have signed 287(g) agreements with ICE. All ten signed in the past six months. It is unclear how many are authorized to conduct welfare checks on immigrant children, or what their geographic limits are.

According to a Facebook post by emergency services, there was an attempted suicide at the Moshannon ICE detention camp last night. Appears services were delayed due to landing zone issues.
